name: eggs, liver and oysters
title: Ray Peat on eggs, liver and oysters
question: Why did he recommend liver and oysters?
description: What Ray Peat thought of eggs, liver and oysters: sources of vitamin A, copper and zinc, how to cook them and why he combined them in his diet.
intro: For Ray Peat, eggs, liver and shellfish worked as a "shotgun" approach: three foods that cover deficiencies you do not even know you have [1]. They supply above all vitamin A, B vitamins and minerals such as copper and zinc [2][3]. Even so, he had qualifications about how to cook them and about the iron in some shellfish [4][5].

sections.heading: A combination to cover what we don't know
paragraphs: According to Peat, calculating nutrients one by one is too complicated. Sometimes a single supplement rescues someone in a serious state, but that kind of luck is rare [1]. That is why he argued for the combination of eggs, liver and shellfish, which serves to fill in what is unknown [1].
The daily menu he proposes in a book addressed to women includes an egg at breakfast and an oyster stew at dinner [6].

sections.heading: Eggs and liver as sources of vitamin A
paragraphs: Peat held that one serving of liver a week, one or two eggs a day and milk are enough to cover vitamin A for most people [2]. For him, any liver (fish, chicken or beef) is a great source, and so are eggs, milk and cheese [7].

He added that vitamin B12 is essential for turning carotene into vitamin A [7]. He also explained that, together with thyroid hormone, vitamin A is the main cofactor for converting cholesterol into hormones [8]. In his opinion, carotene accumulated in excess competes with the enzymes that use vitamin A and ends up acting as an anti-vitamin A [8].

sections.heading: How he preferred eggs, and cholesterol
paragraphs: Peat noted that something in raw yolk has a germicidal effect and helps disinfect the intestine. Cooking reduces that effect, but almost all of the benefit is kept [5]. Even so, he recommended cooking eggs as little as possible, with the yolk runny, because its polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) oxidize and are easily damaged by heat [5].

On cholesterol, he cited studies in which adding eggs to the diet did not worsen the atherogenic character of LDL. One of them, with Mexican children who ate two eggs a day, found that the ratio of LDL to HDL was maintained [9]. He also considered yolk a top-quality protein for refeeding malnourished people, sometimes together with thyroid hormone [10].

sections.heading: Liver: B vitamins, copper and other nutrients
paragraphs: Peat recommended eating liver once a week for its richness in B vitamins [11][12]. In another book he mentions having it at least twice a week [6]. He also lists it as a food rich in folic acid, copper and ubiquinone [3].

He told the case of a man with a recurring infection to whom he gave liver and vitamins, and who by his account recovered in a few days [13]. He explained that folic acid improves the function of white blood cells and that vitamin A is needed to synthesize proteins and form immune tissue [13]. For him, persistent acne or dandruff suggested a lack of vitamin A [6].

sections.heading: Why liver can be hard to digest
paragraphs: Peat thought the difficulty with liver is mostly due to its low fat content. Its high level of protein sends strong signals to the body and calls for quite a lot of extra sugar, and preferably some saturated fat to slow absorption so that digestion is not stressful [1].

sections.heading: Oysters: copper, zinc and the iron problem
paragraphs: According to Peat, oysters are a source of zinc, a mineral he linked to immunity, wound healing, fertility and the nerves [3]. He held that a lack of copper makes tissues retain too much iron, and so he advised regularly eating copper-rich foods such as shrimp and oysters [14][15].

He valued copper because it allows oxygen to be used well to produce energy, keeps the skin and blood vessels elastic and takes part in hair color [14]. On fish, he said he recommended it only for its reliable trace minerals, such as selenium and iodine, and he preferred shellfish and low-fat fish [4]. He qualified this by noting that oysters have a lot of iron and that squid is a very good option, since it is low in iron and rich in copper [4].

faq.q: How much liver did Ray Peat recommend eating?
faq.a: In his writing he speaks of one serving of liver a week, for its B vitamin content [11][12][2]. In another book he mentions having it at least twice a week [6]. According to Peat, that weekly serving together with one or two eggs a day and milk covers vitamin A for most people [2].

faq.q: Why did Ray Peat recommend oysters?
faq.a: He considered them a source of zinc, and shellfish in general a source of copper [3][4]. He held that a lack of copper leads tissues to accumulate iron, which for him was harmful [14]. He also warned that oysters have a lot of iron, and pointed to squid as a low-iron alternative [4].

faq.q: Did Ray Peat think eggs raise cholesterol?
faq.a: He cited studies in which eating eggs did not worsen the atherogenic character of LDL [9]. In one carried out with Mexican children, two eggs a day maintained the ratio of LDL to HDL [9]. For Peat, moreover, vitamin A is needed, together with thyroid hormone, to convert cholesterol into hormones [8].

faq.q: How did Ray Peat prefer to cook eggs?
faq.a: He preferred to cook them as little as possible, with the yolk still runny [5]. According to him, the polyunsaturated fats (PUFA) in the yolk oxidize and are easily damaged by heat, although a cooked egg keeps almost all of the benefit [5].
